question: Does income relate to emissions per person?
week1: Planned. A preliminary rank correlation of 0.857 on 197 countries.
week2: Yes. Rank correlation 0.855 (0.802 to 0.893) across 198 countries; holds under all 4 robustness checks.
week3: Income per person is the strongest model feature (shuffling it costs 0.179 of PR-AUC).
note: All three lenses point the same way.

question: Do income groups differ?
week1: Planned a group comparison; no result.
week2: Yes. Median CO2 per person rises from 0.16 to 6.86 tonnes across the four groups; high income is 14.1 times lower-middle plus low income.
week3: Decoupling windows differ sharply: 43% in high-income countries against 10% to 15% elsewhere.
note: The group effect is partly built in, because groups are defined from income.

question: Have rich countries decoupled?
week1: Planned a decoupling quadrant plot; no result.
week2: Mostly. 64% of high-income countries decoupled against 5% to 20% elsewhere. Median change -15.9%, with CO2 per person down in 50 of 74.
week3: On average 37% of high-income countries decouple in a three-year window (21% for the first window, 56% for the last).
agreement: Agree, with a gap in strength
note: Two different 'decoupling' numbers are not in conflict: one compares two end years, the other three-year windows.

question: What predicts decoupling?
week2: Income group (Cramer's V 0.53). Not tested beyond that.
week3: Income level carries most of the signal. Momentum alone adds nothing (PR-AUC 0.255 against 0.249 for no skill). A free income-group rule scores 0.379, close to the model's 0.390.
agreement: Agree on income; beyond income, weak
note: Beyond income, a country's next three years are hard to predict.

question: Do structural drivers matter?
week2: Exploratory. Industry share adds explanatory power (about 2.2% more CO2 per person per extra point); urbanisation does not clearly.
week3: Oil share and industry share carry some signal; urbanisation matters in cross-validation but not on the test set (0.002).
note: Low confidence: exploratory, predictive rather than causal, and the weeks disagree on urbanisation.
